title: The Station Stack
theme: Describe the whole station declaratively with Compose

missions.title: Write It Down Once
missions.story:
Taped to the rack, in Tomasz's tiny handwriting:

"After every power blip I retype the same docker run line from memory. Last night I got the port wrong and the crew stared at a blank dashboard until breakfast.

Ingrid says the whole station should live in ONE file. Start with the dashboard. `restart-dashboard.sh` shows what I type; the hand-started container `dashboard-hand` is still sitting on port 8090. Please replace it with a Compose project named `station`, so one command brings the dashboard back every time. -- T.W."
objectives: Remove the hand-started container `dashboard-hand`
Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` with the top-level project name `station`
Define a service `dashboard` from `nginx:alpine`, publishing host port 8090 to container port 80 and mounting `./dashboard` read-only at `/usr/share/nginx/html`
Bring the project up in the background so http://localhost:8090 shows the dashboard
missions.startingState: `/workspace/dashboard/index.html` and Tomasz's `restart-dashboard.sh` exist; container `dashboard-hand` is already serving the page on port 8090.
hints: Compose lets you describe containers in a YAML file instead of typing `docker run` flags. The file is called `compose.yaml`, and a single `docker compose` command in that folder reads it. Port 8090 is taken, so deal with the old container first.

The file has two top-level keys: `name:` (the project name) and `services:`. Under a service you list `image`, a `ports` list written as "host:container", and `volumes` where a trailing `:ro` makes the mount read-only. Remove the old container with `docker rm -f`, then start the project with `docker compose up -d`.

Put this in `compose.yaml`, then run `docker rm -f dashboard-hand && docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
name: station
services:
  dashboard:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8090:80"
    volumes:
      - ./dashboard:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro
```

files.content:
KESTREL DASHBOARD

Power: nominal. Wind: 41 km/h. Ice: stable.

#!/bin/sh
# Tomasz: typed from memory after every power blip
docker rm -f dashboard-hand
docker run -d --name dashboard-hand -p 8090:80 \
  -v /workspace/dashboard:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro nginx:alpine

validation.description: Compose project `station` has a running `dashboard` service
The dashboard content is mounted read-only at `/usr/share/nginx/html`

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: station
services:
  dashboard:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8090:80"
    volumes:
      - ./dashboard:/usr/share/nginx/html:ro
EOF
missions.debrief: A compose.yaml turns a pile of remembered flags into a file you can read, review and version: `docker compose up -d` always rebuilds the same state, and the `name:` key decides which project owns the containers. Pro tip: `docker compose config` prints the fully resolved file, which is the fastest way to catch YAML mistakes before anything starts.

missions.title: Two Services, One File
missions.story:
**#kestrel-dev, 02:14**

Amara: the hit counter works on my laptop!!

Amara: it needs redis. `app/app.py` reads `REDIS_HOST` from the environment. I was running redis in a tmux pane. don't ask.

Amara: can you put both in one compose file? project name `weather-desk`. the API is `api` on port 8100, redis is `cache`, and api shouldn't start before cache exists. I'm going to sleep.
objectives: Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` for the project `weather-desk`
Service `cache` runs `redis:7-alpine`
Service `api` runs `python:3.12-alpine` with command `python /app/app.py`, mounts `./app` at `/app` read-only, publishes 8100 to 8000, sets `REDIS_HOST=cache` and declares `depends_on: cache`
Start the project so http://localhost:8100 returns the hit counter
missions.startingState: `/workspace/app/app.py` is Amara's counter service; nothing is running yet.
hints: Both programs go into one `compose.yaml` under `services:`. Services on the same Compose project can reach each other by service name, so the API only needs the right hostname handed to it as an environment variable.

Give `api` an `environment:` block whose value is the name of the redis service, and a `depends_on:` list so Compose starts `cache` first. Because the code lives in `./app`, mount that folder and set `command:` to run the script from the mounted path.

A full file for this mission looks like this. Save it as `compose.yaml` and run `docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
name: weather-desk
services:
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: python /app/app.py
    volumes:
      - ./app:/app:ro
    ports:
      - "8100:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: cache
    depends_on:
      - cache
```

files.content:
import os, socket
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

HOST = os.environ["REDIS_HOST"]


def bump():
    with socket.create_connection((HOST, 6379), timeout=2) as s:
        s.sendall(b"INCR hits\r\n")
        return int(s.recv(64).strip()[1:])


class Desk(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        body = f"WEATHER DESK hits={bump()}\n".encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)


HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), Desk).serve_forever()

params.command: docker compose -p weather-desk exec -T api printenv REDIS_HOST

validation.description: http://localhost:8100 returns the hit counter from redis

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: weather-desk
services:
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: python /app/app.py
    volumes:
      - ./app:/app:ro
    ports:
      - "8100:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: cache
    depends_on:
      - cache
EOF
missions.debrief: Compose gives every project its own network where each service name is a DNS name, so `REDIS_HOST: cache` is all the wiring the API needs. Pro tip: `depends_on` only orders container start, not readiness -- if the dependency needs time to become usable, pair it with a healthcheck.

missions.title: Build on Arrival
missions.story:
```
[nightly] 03:00:01 docker build -t ingest-dev ./ingest      OK
[nightly] 03:00:09 docker run -d -p 8110:8000 kestrel/ingest:dev
[nightly] 03:00:09 Unable to find image 'kestrel/ingest:dev' locally
[nightly] 03:00:10 docker: pull access denied for kestrel/ingest
[nightly] 03:00:10 FATAL: ingest bay is dark
```

Ingrid pinned this above the coffee machine. Amara's nightly script builds one tag and runs another, so the ingest bay for the radiometer data has been dark for three nights. She wants build and run to stop disagreeing: a Compose project `ingest-bay` with one service `ingest`, built from the `./ingest` folder and tagged `kestrel/ingest:dev`.
objectives: Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` for project `ingest-bay`
Service `ingest` builds from `./ingest` and is tagged `kestrel/ingest:dev`
It publishes host port 8110 to container port 8000
Run it so image `kestrel/ingest:dev` exists and http://localhost:8110 answers
missions.startingState: `/workspace/ingest/` holds a working Dockerfile and `app.py`; no image has been built.
hints: A Compose service can carry a `build:` instruction instead of only pulling an image, so Compose builds it for you during `up`. If the service also has an `image:` key, that key becomes the name the built image receives.
Under the service use `build: ./ingest` (the folder containing the Dockerfile) together with `image: kestrel/ingest:dev`. Then `docker compose up -d --build` builds and starts it in one go.

Save this as `compose.yaml` and run `docker compose up -d --build`:

```yaml
name: ingest-bay
services:
  ingest:
    build: ./ingest
    image: kestrel/ingest:dev
    ports:
      - "8110:8000"
```

files.content:
FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /srv
COPY app.py .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer


class Bay(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b"INGEST READY: radiometer feed open\n")


HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), Bay).serve_forever()

validation.description: http://localhost:8110 reports the ingest bay is ready

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: ingest-bay
services:
  ingest:
    build: ./ingest
    image: kestrel/ingest:dev
    ports:
      - "8110:8000"
EOF
missions.debrief: With `build:` plus `image:`, Compose is the single source of truth for both how an image is made and what it is called, so scripts can no longer drift apart. Pro tip: `docker compose build` only builds, and `docker compose up -d --build` forces a rebuild after you edit code -- plain `up` reuses an existing image.

missions.title: Wait for the Database
missions.story:
[RADIO -- PETREL, CHANNEL 9]

Rafael Duarte: Kestrel Point, Petrel. I sail at dawn and my cargo manifest has to be in your database before I load. Last time the migration ran while Postgres was still starting, the table never got made, and I loaded half the crates blind. Over.

Ingrid, from the doorway: Compose project `manifest`, engineer. Service `db` is Postgres, container name `manifest-db`, with a health check. Service `migrate` runs `migrations/001_cargo.sql` once the database is healthy, then exits cleanly. The tide won't wait. Over.
objectives: Create `/workspace/compose.yaml` for project `manifest`
Service `db` runs `postgres:16-alpine` with `container_name: manifest-db`, a `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, and a healthcheck
Service `migrate` runs `psql` against host `db` with the file `/migrations/001_cargo.sql` (mount `./migrations`), starts only when `db` is healthy and exits with code 0
Bring the project up: `manifest-db` is healthy and table `cargo_manifest` contains 3 rows
missions.startingState: `/workspace/migrations/001_cargo.sql` creates and fills `cargo_manifest`; there is no compose file yet.
hints: A container being 'started' is not the same as the service inside it being ready. Compose can wait for a health check: give `db` a `healthcheck`, and make `migrate` depend on it with a condition rather than just a name.

Use `pg_isready` as the health test and `depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy` on the migrator. The migrator can reuse the Postgres image just for its `psql` client; give it `PGPASSWORD` and set `restart: "no"` so it exits once and stays done. Use `-h 127.0.0.1` in the health test so it only turns healthy when Postgres accepts network connections.

A complete file, followed by `docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
name: manifest
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: manifest-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
  migrate:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    volumes:
      - ./migrations:/migrations:ro
    command: ["psql", "-h", "db", "-U", "postgres", "-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "-f", "/migrations/001_cargo.sql"]
    restart: "no"
```

validation.description: The one-shot `migrate` container finished with exit code 0

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: manifest
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    container_name: manifest-db
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 20
  migrate:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      PGPASSWORD: kestrel-pass
    volumes:
      - ./migrations:/migrations:ro
    command: ["psql", "-h", "db", "-U", "postgres", "-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "-f", "/migrations/001_cargo.sql"]
    restart: "no"
EOF
missions.debrief: `condition: service_healthy` makes the migrator wait for the moment the database actually answers, not just the moment its process starts. Pro tip: write migrations with `IF NOT EXISTS`, so rerunning the one-shot service is harmless.

missions.title: Many Hands
missions.story:
NORA: SURVEY-QUEUE BACKLOG 412 JOBS
NORA: SURVEY-WORKER COUNT 1. EXPECTED 3
NORA: CPU HEADROOM 71 PERCENT. IDLE

The glacier survey pipeline (Compose project `survey`) has a `queue` and a single `worker`. The jobs are independent; three workers would clear the backlog before the shift ends. Amara tried to scale it and got a name conflict, because the compose file pins a container name and a host port on the worker. Fix the file so `docker compose up -d` leaves exactly three `worker` containers, and do not disturb the `queue`.
objectives: Edit `/workspace/compose.yaml` so service `worker` has no fixed `container_name` and no published host port
Project `survey` runs exactly 3 containers of service `worker` (via `deploy.replicas` or `--scale`)
Service `queue` keeps running
missions.startingState: Project `survey` is up with one `survey-worker` (host port 8200) and a redis `queue`.
hints: Compose names containers `project-service-N` so they can be numbered. A hard-coded `container_name` allows only one copy, and a fixed host port can be bound by only one container, so both must go before a service can have several replicas.

Delete the `container_name:` line and the `ports:` section from `worker`, then ask for three copies, either with `deploy: replicas: 3` in the file or with `docker compose up -d --scale worker=3` on the command line.

The worker section should end up like this, then run `docker compose up -d`:

```yaml
  worker:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
    deploy:
      replicas: 3
```

files.content:
name: survey
services:
  queue:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  worker:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    container_name: survey-worker
    command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
    ports:
      - "8200:8000"

validation.description: `worker` no longer publishes fixed host port 8200
Exactly 3 `worker` containers are running in project `survey`

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: survey
services:
  queue:
    image: redis:7-alpine
  worker:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
    deploy:
      replicas: 3
EOF
missions.debrief: Anything that must be unique per container -- a fixed container name or a fixed host port -- blocks horizontal scaling; stateless workers should be anonymous and reached through the project network. Pro tip: `docker compose up -d --scale worker=5` changes the count on the fly, but `deploy.replicas` keeps the number written down in the file.

missions.title: Front Door, Back Room
missions.story:
FRONT-DOOR CHECKLIST -- Ingrid Halvorsen, unsigned

[ ] Crew traffic enters through `proxy` on port 8120 and nowhere else.
[ ] `db` lives in the back room: `proxy` must have no route to it, ever.
[ ] `api` is the only service allowed to stand in both rooms.

Right now all three services share one flat network, so a compromised proxy could talk straight to the database. Rework the stack in Compose project `frontdoor` with two networks, `front` and `back`, and bring it up again. Tick every box.
objectives: In `/workspace/compose.yaml` (project `frontdoor`) define networks `front` and `back`
`proxy` joins only `front`; `db` joins only `back`; `api` joins both
The stack runs, and http://localhost:8120 returns the API answer including `db=PONG`
From inside `proxy`, the hostname `db` must not resolve
missions.startingState: Project `frontdoor` runs with `proxy`, `api` and `db` all on Compose's default flat network.
hints: Compose creates one default network for a project, and every service on it can see every other. Containers can only resolve each other when they share at least one network, so segmentation means declaring your own networks and attaching each service only where it belongs.

Add a top-level `networks:` section with `front` and `back`, and a `networks:` list under every service. Once every service lists networks explicitly, the default one disappears. Then apply the change with `docker compose up -d`.

Keep the services you have and add the network wiring:

```yaml
services:
  proxy:
    networks: [front]
  api:
    networks: [front, back]
  db:
    networks: [back]
networks:
  front:
  back:
```

files.content:
name: frontdoor
services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8120:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - api
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "/app/app.py"]
    volumes:
      - ./api:/app:ro
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
  db:
    image: redis:7-alpine

params.command: docker inspect -f '{{range $k,$v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' $(docker ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=frontdoor --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=proxy) | xargs -n1 | sort | xargs

validation.description: `proxy` is attached only to the `front` network

params.command: docker inspect -f '{{range $k,$v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' $(docker ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=frontdoor --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=api) | xargs -n1 | sort | xargs

docker inspect -f '{{range $k,$v := .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{$k}} {{end}}' $(docker ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=frontdoor --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=db) | xargs -n1 | sort | xargs

validation.description: `db` is attached only to the `back` network
The API can still reach the database through the proxy

params.command: docker compose -p frontdoor exec -T proxy sh -c 'getent hosts db || echo UNREACHABLE'

validation.description: From inside `proxy`, the name `db` does not resolve

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: frontdoor
services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8120:80"
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on:
      - api
    networks: [front]
  api:
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["python", "/app/app.py"]
    volumes:
      - ./api:/app:ro
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
    networks: [front, back]
  db:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    networks: [back]
networks:
  front:
  back:
EOF
missions.debrief: Multiple networks turn a flat 'everything talks to everything' layout into rooms with doors: only the service standing in both rooms can carry traffic between them. Pro tip: mark a network `internal: true` in Compose to also cut it off from the outside world.

missions.title: Settings Without Edits
missions.story:
**From:** Amara Okafor
**Subject:** lab-bench, again

Three people edited `compose.yaml` this week just to change a port, and Kip's `toolbox` debug container has been running on the bench for days eating CPU.

Please move the tunables into a `.env` file next to `compose.yaml`: `DESK_PORT=8130` and `DESK_TAG=1.27-alpine`, and make the `desk` service use them. `toolbox` should only exist when somebody asks for the `debug` profile. Project name stays `lab-bench`.

Thanks!! -- A.
objectives: Create `/workspace/.env` with `DESK_PORT=8130` and `DESK_TAG=1.27-alpine`
In `compose.yaml`, build the `desk` image name and host port from `${DESK_TAG}` and `${DESK_PORT}`
Put `toolbox` in the profile `debug`, and make sure no `toolbox` container is running
Project `lab-bench` serves http://localhost:8130 from `nginx:1.27-alpine`
missions.startingState: Project `lab-bench` is running with hard-coded values: `desk` on `nginx:alpine` (port 8000) and an always-on `toolbox`.
hints: Compose reads a file named `.env` in the project folder and substitutes `${VARIABLE}` references inside `compose.yaml`. Separately, a service can be tagged with `profiles`, which keeps it out of a plain `docker compose up` until that profile is requested.

In `.env` write one `KEY=value` per line. In the YAML use `nginx:${DESK_TAG}` and `"${DESK_PORT}:80"`, and add `profiles: ["debug"]` under `toolbox`. Editing the file does not stop the toolbox that is already running; remove it explicitly with `docker compose rm -sf toolbox`.

Put this into `.env`:

```bash
DESK_PORT=8130
DESK_TAG=1.27-alpine
```

and edit `compose.yaml` so it reads:

```yaml
name: lab-bench
services:
  desk:
    image: nginx:${DESK_TAG}
    ports:
      - "${DESK_PORT}:80"
  toolbox:
    image: alpine:3.20
    command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
    profiles: ["debug"]
```

Finish with `docker compose rm -sf toolbox` and `docker compose up -d`.

files.content:
name: lab-bench
services:
  desk:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8000:80"
  toolbox:
    image: alpine:3.20
    command: ["sleep", "infinity"]

validation.description: `compose.yaml` references `${DESK_PORT}` instead of a hard-coded port
`compose.yaml` references `${DESK_TAG}` instead of a hard-coded tag
`toolbox` is only part of the project when the `debug` profile is requested

solution:
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: lab-bench
services:
  desk:
    image: nginx:${DESK_TAG}
    ports:
      - "${DESK_PORT}:80"
  toolbox:
    image: alpine:3.20
    command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
    profiles: ["debug"]
EOF
missions.debrief: Keeping tunables in `.env` means a port or tag change is a one-line edit that never touches the structure of the stack, and a profile keeps tools like a debug toolbox off until someone asks for them. Pro tip: `docker compose --profile debug up -d toolbox` starts it on demand, and `${VAR:-default}` supplies a fallback when the variable is missing.
